entries.486bf7f429b6a4907cb877b2fa8f342417be6b32: <div sID="gen11057" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="38" osisID="Ps.38" sID="Ps.38"/> <div eID="gen11057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11058" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11059" type="x-p"/> This is one of the penitential psalms; it is full of grief and complaint from the beginning to the end. David's sins and his afflictions are the cause of his grief and the matter of his complaints. It should seem he was now sick and in pain, which reminded him of his sins and helped to humble him for them; he was, at the same time, deserted by his friends and persecuted by his enemies; so that the psalm is calculated for the depth of distress and a complication of calamities. He complains, I. Of God's displeasure, and of his own sin which provoked God against him, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.1-Ps.38.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. Of his bodily sickness, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.6-Ps.38.10">ver. 6-10</reference>. III. Of the unkindness of his friends, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.11">ver. 11</reference>. IV. Of the injuries which his enemies did him, pleading his good conduct towards them, yet confessing his sins against God, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.12-Ps.38.20">ver. 12-20</reference>. Lastly, he concludes the psalm with earnest prayers to God for his gracious presence and help, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.21-Ps.38.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>. In singing this psalm we ought to be much affected with the malignity of sin; and, if we have not such troubles as are here described, we know not how soon we may have, and therefore must sing of them by way of preparation and we know that others have them, and therefore we must sing of the by way of sympathy.
entries.e9e91df4860899acd240598320d1e529fb397d74: <div eID="gen11059" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11058" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sorrowful Complaints.</title> <div sID="gen11060" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , rebuke me not in thy wrath: neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure. 2 For thine arrows stick fast in me, and thy hand presseth me sore. <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger; neither <hi type="italic">is there any</hi> rest in my bones because of my sin. <hi type="super">4</hi> For mine iniquities are gone over mine head: as a heavy burden they are too heavy for me. <hi type="super">5</hi> My wounds stink <hi type="italic">and</hi> are corrupt because of my foolishness. 6 I am troubled; I am bowed down greatly; I go mourning all the day long. <hi type="super">7</hi> For my loins are filled with a loathsome <hi type="italic">disease:</hi> and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no soundness in my flesh. 8 I am feeble and sore broken: I have roared by reason of the disquietness of my heart. <hi type="super">9</hi> Lord, all my desire <hi type="italic">is</hi> before thee; and my groaning is not hid from thee. <hi type="super">10</hi> My heart panteth, my strength faileth me: as for the light of mine eyes, it also is gone from me. <hi type="super">11</hi> My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off. <div eID="gen11060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11061" type="x-p"/> The title of this psalm is very observable; it is a psalm <hi type="italic">to bring to remembrance;</hi> the 70th psalm, which was likewise penned in a day of affliction, is so entitled. It is designed, 1. To bring to his own remembrance. We will suppose it penned when he was sick and in pain, and then it teaches us that times of sickness are times to bring to remembrance, to bring the sin to remembrance, for which God contended with us, to awaken our consciences to deal faithfully and plainly with us, and set our sins in order before us, for our humiliation. <hi type="italic">In a day of adversity consider.</hi> Or we may suppose it penned after his recovery, but designed as a record of the convictions he was under and the workings of his heart when he was in affliction, that upon every review of this psalm he might call to mind the good impressions then made upon him and make a fresh improvement of them. To the same purport was the writing of Hezekiah when he had been sick. 2. To put others in mind of the same things which he was himself mindful of, and to teach them what to think and what to say when they are sick and in affliction; let them think as he did, and speak as he did. <div eID="gen11061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11062" type="x-p"/> I. He deprecates the wrath of God and his displeasure in his affliction (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">O Lord! rebuke me not in thy wrath.</hi> With this same petition he began another prayer for the visitation of the sick, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1">Ps. vi. 1</reference>. This was most upon his heart, and should be most upon ours when we are in affliction, that, however God rebukes and chastens us, it may not be in wrath and displeasure, for that will be wormwood and gall in the affliction and misery. Those that would escape the wrath of God must pray against that more than any outward affliction, and be content to bear any outward affliction while it comes from, and consists with, the love of God. <div eID="gen11062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11063" type="x-p"/> II. He bitterly laments the impressions of God's displeasure upon his soul (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy arrows stick fast in me.</hi> Let Job's complaint (<reference osisRef="Job.7.4">ch. vii. 4</reference>) expound this of David. By the arrows of the Almighty he means the terrors of God, which did set themselves in array against him. He was under a very melancholy frightful apprehension of the wrath of God against him for his sins, and thought he could look for nothing but judgment and fiery indignation to devour him. God's arrows, as they are sure to hit the mark, so they are sure to stick where they hit, to stick fast, till he is pleased to draw them out and to bind up with his comforts the wound he has made with his terrors. This will be the everlasting misery of the damned—the arrows of God's wrath will stick fast in them and the wound will be incurable. "<hi type="italic">Thy hand,</hi> thy heavy hand, <hi type="italic">presses me sore,</hi> and I am ready to sink under it; it not only lies hard upon me, but it lies long; and who knows the power of God's anger, the weight of his hand?" Sometimes God shot his arrows, and stretched forth his hand, for David (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.4">Ps. xviii. 14</reference>), but now against him; so uncertain is the continuance of divine comforts, where yet the continuance of divine grace is assured. He complains of God's wrath as that which inflicted the bodily distemper he was under (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is no soundness in my flesh because of thy anger.</hi> The bitterness of it, infused in his mind, affected his body; but that was not the worst: it caused the disquietude of his heart, by reason of which he forgot the courage of a soldier, the dignity of a prince, and all the cheerfulness of the sweet psalmist of Israel, and roared terribly, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.8">v. 8</reference>. Nothing will disquiet the heart of a good man so much as the sense of God's anger, which shows what a fearful thing it is to fall into his hands. The way to keep the heart quiet is to keep ourselves in the love of God and to do nothing to offend him. <div eID="gen11063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11064" type="x-p"/> III. He acknowledges his sin to be the procuring provoking cause of all his troubles, and groans more under the load of guilt than any other load, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.3">v. 3</reference>. He complains that his flesh had no soundness, his bones had no rest, so great an agitation he was in. "It is <hi type="italic">because of thy anger;</hi> that kindles the fire which burns so fiercely;" but, in the next words, he justifies God herein, and takes all the blame upon himself: "It is <hi type="italic">because of my sin.</hi> I have deserved it, and so have brought it upon myself. My own iniquities do correct me." If our trouble be the fruit of God's anger, we may thank ourselves; it is our sin that is the cause of it. Are we restless? It is sin that makes us so. If there were not sin in our souls, there would be no pain in our bones, no illness in our bodies. It is sin therefore that this good man complains most of, 1. As a burden, a heavy burden (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My iniquities have gone over my head,</hi> as proud waters over a man that is sinking and drowning, or as a heavy burden upon my head, pressing me down more than I am able to bear or to bear up under." Note, Sin is a burden. The power of sin dwelling in us is a weight, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">Heb. xii. 1</reference>. All are clogged with it; it keeps men from soaring upward and pressing forward. All the saints are complaining of it as a body of death they are loaded with, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.24">Rom. vii. 24</reference>. The guilt of sin committed by us is a burden, a heavy burden; it is a burden to God (he is pressed under it, <reference osisRef="Amos.2.13">Amos ii. 13</reference>), a burden to the whole creation, which groans under it, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.21-Rom.8.22">Rom. viii. 21, 22</reference>. It will, first or last, be a burden to the sinner himself, either a burden of repentance when he is pricked to the heart for it, labours, and is heavy-laden, under it, or a burden of ruin when it sinks him to the lowest hell and will for ever detain him there; it will be a talent of lead upon him, <reference osisRef="Zech.5.8">Zech. v. 8</reference>. Sinners are said to bear their iniquity. Threatenings are burdens. 2. As wounds, dangerous wounds (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My wounds stink and are corrupt</hi> (as wounds in the body rankle, and fester, and grow foul, for want of being dressed and looked after), and it is through my own <hi type="italic">foolishness.</hi>" Sins are wounds (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.23">Gen. iv. 23</reference>), painful mortal wounds. Our wounds by sin are often in a bad condition, no care taken of them, no application made to them, and it is owing to the sinner's foolishness in not confessing sin, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.3-Ps.32.4">Ps. xxxii. 3, 4</reference>. A slight sore, neglected, may prove of fatal consequence, and so may a slight sin slighted and left unrepented of. <div eID="gen11064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11065" type="x-p"/> IV. He bemoans himself because of his afflictions, and gives ease to his grief by giving vent to it and pouring out his complaint before the Lord. <div eID="gen11065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11066" type="x-p"/> 1. He was troubled in mind, his conscience was pained, and he had no rest in his own spirit; and a wounded spirit who can bear? He was <hi type="italic">troubled,</hi> or distorted, <hi type="italic">bowed down greatly,</hi> and went <hi type="italic">mourning all the day long,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.6">v. 6</reference>. He was always pensive and melancholy, which made him a burden and terror to himself. His spirit was feeble and sorely broken, and his heart disquieted, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.8">v. 8</reference>. Herein David, in his sufferings, was a type of Christ, who, being in his agony, cried out, <hi type="italic">My soul is exceedingly sorrowful.</hi> This is a sorer affliction than any other in this world; whatever God is pleased to lay upon us, we have no reason to complain as long as he preserves to us the use of our reason and the peace of our consciences. <div eID="gen11066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11067" type="x-p"/> 2. He was sick and weak in body; his loins were filled with a loathsome disease, some swelling, or ulcer, or inflammation (some think a plague-sore, such as Hezekiah's boil), and there was <hi type="italic">no soundness in his flesh,</hi> but, like Job, he was all over distempered. See (1.) What vile bodies these are which we carry about with us, what grievous diseases they are liable to, and what an offence and grievance they may soon be made by some diseases to the souls that animate them, as they always are a cloud and clog. (2.) That the bodies both of the greatest and of the best of men have in them the same seeds of diseases that the bodies of others have, and are liable to the same disasters. David himself, though so great a prince and so great a saint, was not exempt from the most grievous diseases: there was no soundness even in his flesh. Probably this was after his sin in the matter of Uriah, and thus did he smart in his flesh for his fleshly lusts. When, at any time, we are distempered in our bodies, we ought to remember how God has been dishonoured in and by our bodies. He was <hi type="italic">feeble and sorely broken,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.8">v. 8</reference>. His <hi type="italic">heart panted,</hi> and was in a continual palpitation, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.10">v. 10</reference>. His <hi type="italic">strength</hi> and limbs <hi type="italic">failed</hi> him. As for <hi type="italic">the light of his eyes,</hi> that <hi type="italic">had gone from him,</hi> either with much weeping or by a defluxion of rheum upon them, or perhaps through the lowness of his spirits and the frequent returns of fainting. Note, Sickness will tame the strongest body and the stoutest spirit. David was famed for his courage and great exploits; and yet, when God contended with him by bodily sickness and the impressions of his wrath upon his mind, his hair is cut, his heart fails him, and he becomes weak as water. Therefore let not the strongman glory in his strength, nor any man set grief at defiance, however it may be thought at a distance. <div eID="gen11067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11068" type="x-p"/> 3. His friends were unkind to him (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">My lovers</hi> (such as had been merry with him in the day of his mirth) now <hi type="italic">stand aloof from my sore;</hi> they would not sympathize with him in his griefs, nor so much as come within hearing of his complaints, but, like the priest and Levite (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.31">Luke x. 31</reference>), <hi type="italic">passed on the other side.</hi> Even <hi type="italic">his kinsmen,</hi> that were bound to him by blood and alliance, <hi type="italic">stood afar off.</hi> See what little reason we have to trust in man or to wonder if we disappointed in our expectations of kindness from men. Adversity tries friendship, and separates between the precious and the vile. It is our wisdom to make sure a friend in heaven, who will not stand aloof from our sore and from whose love no tribulation nor distress shall be able to separate us. David, in his troubles, was a type of Christ in his agony, Christ, on his cross, feeble and sorely broken, and then deserted by his friends and kinsmen, who beheld afar off. <div eID="gen11068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11069" type="x-p"/> V. In the midst of his complaints, he comforts himself with the cognizance God graciously took both of his griefs and of his prayers (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lord, all my desire is before thee.</hi> Thou knowest what I want and what I would have: <hi type="italic">My groaning is not hidden from thee.</hi> Thou knowest the burdens I groan under and the blessings I groan after." The <hi type="italic">groanings which cannot be uttered</hi> are not hidden from him that <hi type="italic">searches the heart and knows what is the mind of the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26-Rom.8.27">Rom. viii. 26, 27</reference>. <div eID="gen11069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11070" type="x-p"/> In singing this, and praying it over, whatever burden lies upon our spirits, we would by faith cast it upon God, and all our care concerning it, and then be easy.
entries.7dbe6c53bd20bbe32cae9e9014ca09ed10aa194c: <div eID="gen11070" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Sorrowful Complaints.</title> <div sID="gen11071" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> They also that seek after my life lay snares <hi type="italic">for me:</hi> and they that seek my hurt speak mischievous things, and imagine deceits all the day long. <hi type="super">13</hi> But I, as a deaf <hi type="italic">man,</hi> heard not; and <hi type="italic">I was</hi> as a dumb man <hi type="italic">that</hi> openeth not his mouth. <hi type="super">14</hi> Thus I was as a man that heareth not, and in whose mouth <hi type="italic">are</hi> no reproofs. <hi type="super">15</hi> For in thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , do I hope: thou wilt hear, O Lord my God. <hi type="super">16</hi> For I said, <hi type="italic">Hear me,</hi> lest <hi type="italic">otherwise</hi> they should rejoice over me: when my foot slippeth, they magnify <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> against me. <hi type="super">17</hi> For I <hi type="italic">am</hi> ready to halt, and my sorrow <hi type="italic">is</hi> continually before me. <hi type="super">18</hi> For I will declare mine iniquity; I will be sorry for my sin. <hi type="super">19</hi> But mine enemies <hi type="italic">are</hi> lively, <hi type="italic">and</hi> they are strong: and they that hate me wrongfully are multiplied. <hi type="super">20</hi> They also that render evil for good are mine adversaries; because I follow <hi type="italic">the thing that</hi> good <hi type="italic">is.</hi> 21 Forsake me not, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : O my God, be not far from me. <hi type="super">22</hi> Make haste to help me, O Lord my salvation. <div eID="gen11071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11072" type="x-p"/> In these verses, <div eID="gen11072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11073" type="x-p"/> I. David complains of the power and malice of his enemies, who, it should seem, not only took occasion from the weakness of his body and the trouble of his mind to insult over him, but took advantage thence to do him a mischief. He has a great deal to say against them, which he humbly offers as a reason why God should appear for him, as <reference osisRef="Ps.25.19">Ps. xxv. 19</reference>, <hi type="italic">Consider my enemies.</hi> 1. "They are very spiteful and cruel: <hi type="italic">They seek my hurt;</hi> nay, they <hi type="italic">seek after my life,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.38.12">v. 12</reference>. That life which was so precious in the sight of the Lord and all good men was aimed at, as if it had been forfeited, or a public nuisance. Such is the enmity of the serpent's seed against the seed of the woman; it would wound the head, though it can but reach the heel. It is the blood of the saints that is thirsted after. 2. "They are very subtle and politic. They <hi type="italic">lay snares,</hi> they <hi type="italic">imagine deceits,</hi> and herein they are restless and unwearied: they do it <hi type="italic">all the day long.</hi> They speak mischievous things one to another; every one has something or other to propose that may be a mischief to me." Mischief, covered and carried on by deceit, may well be called a <hi type="italic">snare.</hi> 3. "They are very insolent and abusive: <hi type="italic">When my foot slips,</hi> when I fall into any trouble, or when I make any mistake, misplace a word, or take a false step, they magnify themselves against me; they are pleased with it, and promise themselves that it will ruin my interest, and that if I slip I shall certainly fall and be undone." 4. "They are not only unjust, but very ungrateful: They <hi type="italic">hate me wrongfully,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.19">v. 19</reference>. I never did them any ill turn, nor so much as bore them any ill-will, nor ever gave them any provocation; nay, <hi type="italic">they render evil for good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.20">v. 20</reference>. Many a kindness I have done them, for which I might have expected a return of kindness; but <hi type="italic">for my love they are my adversaries,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">Ps. cix. 4</reference>. Such a rooted enmity there is in the hearts of wicked men to goodness for its own sake that they hate it, even when they themselves have the benefit of it; they hate prayer even in those that pray for them, and hate peace even in those that would be at peace with them. Very ill-natured indeed those are whom no courtesy will oblige, but who are rather exasperated by it. 5. "They are very impious and devilish: <hi type="italic">They are my adversaries</hi> merely <hi type="italic">because I follow the thing that good is.</hi>" They hated him, not only for his kindness to them, but for his devotion and obedience to God; they hated him because they hated God and all that bear his image. If we suffer ill for doing well, we must not think it strange; from the beginning it was so (Cain slew Abel, because his works were righteous); nor must we think it hard, because it will not be always so; for so much the greater will our reward be. 6. "They are many and mighty: They <hi type="italic">are lively; they are strong; they are multiplied,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.19">v. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Lord, how are those increased that trouble me?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.3.1">Ps. iii. 1</reference>. Holy David was weak and faint; his heart panted, and his strength failed; he was melancholy and of a sorrowful spirit, and persecuted by his friends; but at the same time his wicked enemies were strong and lively, and their number increased. Let us not therefore pretend to judge of men's characters by their outward condition; none knows love or hatred by all that is before him. It should seem that David in this, as in other complaints he makes of his enemies, has an eye to Christ, whose persecutors were such as are here described, perfectly lost to all honour and virtue. None hate Christianity but such as have first divested themselves of the first principles of humanity and broken through its most sacred bonds. <div eID="gen11073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11074" type="x-p"/> II. He reflects, with comfort, upon his own peaceable and pious behaviour under all the injuries and indignities that were done him. It is then only that our enemies do us a real mischief when they provoke us to sin (<reference osisRef="Neh.6.13">Neh. vi. 13</reference>), when they prevail to put us out of the possession of our own souls, and drive us from God and our duty. If by divine grace we are enabled to prevent this mischief, we quench their fiery darts, and are saved from harm. If still we hold fast our integrity and our peace, who can hurt us? This David did here. 1. He kept his temper, and was not ruffled nor discomposed by any of the slights that were put upon him or the mischievous things that were said or done against him (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.13-Ps.38.14">v. 13, 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I, as a deaf man, heard not;</hi> I took no notice of the affronts put upon me, did not resent them, nor was put into disorder by them, much less did I meditate revenge, or study to return the injury." Note, The less notice we take of the unkindness and injuries that are done us the more we consult the quiet of our own minds. Being deaf, he was dumb, as a man <hi type="italic">in whose mouth there are no reproofs;</hi> he was as silent as if he had nothing to say for himself, for fear of putting himself into a heat and incensing his enemies yet more against him; he would not only not recriminate upon them, but not so much as vindicate himself, lest his necessary defence should be construed his offence. Though they sought after his life, and his silence might be taken for a confession of his guilt, yet he was as a dumb man that opens not his mouth. Note, When our enemies are most clamorous it is generally our prudence to be silent, or to say little, lest we make bad worse. David could not hope by his mildness to win upon his enemies, nor by his soft answers to turn away their wrath; for they were men of such base spirits that they rendered him evil for good; and yet he conducted himself thus meekly towards them, that he might prevent his own sin and might have the comfort of it in the reflection. Herein David was a type of Christ, who was as a sheep dumb before the shearer, and, when he was reviled, reviled not again; and both are examples to us not to render railing for railing. 2. He kept close to his God by faith and prayer, and so both supported himself under these injuries and silenced his own resentments of them. (1.) He trusted in God (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I was as a man that opens not his mouth, for in thee, O Lord! do I hope.</hi> I depend upon thee to plead my cause and clear my innocency, and, some way or other, to put my enemies to silence and shame." His lovers and friends, that should have owned him, and stood by him, and appeared as witnesses for him, withdrew from him, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.10">v. 10</reference>. But God is a friend that will never fail us if we hope in him. "<hi type="italic">I was as a man that heareth not, for thou wilt hear.</hi> Why need I hear, and God hear too?" <hi type="italic">He careth for you</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.7">1 Pet. v. 7</reference>), and why need you care and God care too? "<hi type="italic">Thou wilt answer</hi>" (so some) "and therefore I will say nothing." Note, It is a good reason why we should bear reproach and calumny with silence and patience, because God is a witness to all the wrong that is done us, and, in due time, will be a witness for us and against those that do us wrong; therefore let us be silent, because, if we be, then we may expect that God will appear for us, for this is an evidence that we trust in him; but, if we undertake to manage for ourselves, we take God's work out of his hands and forfeit the benefit of his appearing for us. Our Lord Jesus, when he suffered, threatened not, because he <hi type="italic">committed himself to him that judges righteously</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.23">1 Pet. ii. 23</reference>); and we shall lose nothing, at last, by doing so. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt answer, Lord, for me.</hi> (2.) He called upon God (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">For I said,</hi> Hear me (that is supplied); "<hi type="italic">I said so</hi>" (as <reference osisRef="Ps.38.15">v. 15</reference>); "in thee do I hope, for thou wilt hear, lest they should rejoice over me. I comforted myself with that when I was apprehensive that they would overwhelm me." It is a great support to us, when men are false and unkind, that we have a God to go to whom we may be free with and who will be faithful to us. <div eID="gen11074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11075" type="x-p"/> III. He here bewails his own follies and infirmities. 1. He was very sensible of the present workings of corruption in him, and that he was now ready to repine at the providence of God and to be put into a passion by the injuries men did him: <hi type="italic">I am ready to halt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.17">v. 17</reference>. This will best be explained by a reflection like this which the psalmist made upon himself in a similar case (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">Ps. lxxiii. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">My feet were almost gone, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.</hi> So here: <hi type="italic">I was ready to halt,</hi> ready to say, <hi type="italic">I have cleansed my hands in vain.</hi> His sorrow was continual: <hi type="italic">All the day long have I been plagued.</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.13-Ps.73.14">Ps. lxxiii. 13, 14</reference>), and it was continually before him; he could not forbear poring upon it, and that made him almost ready to halt between religion and irreligion. The fear of this drove him to his God: "In thee do I hope, not only that thou wilt plead my cause, but that thou wilt prevent my falling into sin." Good men, by setting their sorrow continually before them, have been ready to halt, who, by setting God always before them, have kept their standing. 2. He remembered against himself his former transgressions, acknowledging that by them he had brought these troubles upon himself and forfeited the divine protection. Though before men he could justify himself, before God he will judge and condemn himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will declare my iniquity,</hi> and not cover it; <hi type="italic">I will be sorry for my sin,</hi> and not make a light matter of it;" and this helped to make him silent under the rebukes of Providence and the reproaches of men. Note, If we be truly penitent for sin, that will make us patient under affliction, and particularly under unjust censures. Two things are required in repentance:—(1.) Confession of sin: "<hi type="italic">I will declare my iniquity;</hi> I will not only in general own myself a sinner, but I will make a particular acknowledgment of what I have done amiss." We must declare our sins before God freely and fully, and with their aggravating circumstances, that we may give glory to God and take shame to ourselves. (2.) Contrition for sin: <hi type="italic">I will be sorry for it.</hi> Sin will have sorrow; every true penitent grieves for the dishonour he has done to God and the wrong he has done to himself. "I will be in care or fear about my sin" (so some), "in fear lest it ruin me and in care to get it pardoned." <div eID="gen11075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11076" type="x-p"/> IV. He concludes with very earnest prayers to God for his gracious presence with him and seasonable powerful succour in his distress (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.21-Ps.38.22">v. 21, 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Forsake me not, O Lord!</hi> though my friends forsake me, and though I deserve to be forsaken by thee. Be not far from me, as my unbelieving heart is ready to fear thou art." Nothing goes nearer to the heart of a good man in affliction than to be under the apprehension of God's deserting him in wrath; nor does any thing therefore come more feelingly from his heart than this prayer: "<hi type="italic">Lord, be not thou far from me; make haste for my help;</hi> for I am ready to perish, and in danger of being lost if relief do not come quickly." God gives us leave, not only to call upon him when we are in trouble, but to hasten him. He pleads, "Thou art <hi type="italic">my God,</hi> whom I serve, and on whom I depend to bear me out; and <hi type="italic">my salvation,</hi> who alone art able to save me, who hast engaged thyself by promise to save me, and from whom alone I expect salvation." Is any afflicted? let him thus pray, let him thus plead, let him thus hope, in singing this psalm.  <chapter eID="Ps.38"/> <div eID="gen11076" type="x-p"/>

entries.dd681859fbcb7d8d0e6d0b497256ab9b18f47be0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5903"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 38</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.38.1-Ps.38.22">Psa 38:1-22</reference>. To bring to remembrance, or, remind God of His mercy and himself of his sin. Appealing to God for relief from His heavy chastisement, the Psalmist avows his integrity before men, complains of the defection of friends and persecution of enemies, and in a submissive spirit, casting himself on God, with penitent confession he pleads God's covenant relation and his innocence of the charges of his enemies, and prays for divine comfort and help.</title> <div sID="gen8976" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5903"/>1-4. He deprecates deserved punishment, which is described (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.1">Psa 6:1</reference>), under the figure of bodily disease [Psa 38:3]. <div eID="gen8976" type="x-p"/>
entries.f81173c9826b8dd9021fb9725bb8f7679e90f317: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5906"/><div sID="gen8980" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5906"/>5-8. The loathsomeness, corruption, and wasting torture of severe physical disease set forth his mental anguish [Psa 38:6]. It is possible some bodily disease was connected. The<div eID="gen8980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8981" type="x-p"/> loins are the seat of strength. His exhaustion left him only the power to groan [Psa 38:9]. <div eID="gen8981" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa9692aa9ab7f09eab48ee9a534ace6cb44c42da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5907"/><div sID="gen8982" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5907"/>9. That God can hear (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Ro 8:26</reference>). <div eID="gen8982" type="x-p"/>
entries.07eda4816bd9b22f1d02753d816a9bed2f2320f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5908"/><div sID="gen8983" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5908"/><hi type="bold">10. My heart panteth--</hi>as if barely surviving.<div eID="gen8983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">light ... from me--</hi>utter exhaustion (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.7">Psa 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.13.3">13:3</reference>). <div eID="gen8984" type="x-p"/>
entries.d96a3ebf83e64f613b4f28bf1a650af35d8c3143: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5909"/><div sID="gen8985" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5909"/>11-12. Friends desert, but foes increase in malignity. <div eID="gen8985" type="x-p"/>
entries.a773758e6751ec9778bd82d3bc1abb0d34dfb86c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5911"/><div sID="gen8987" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5911"/>13-14. He patiently submits, uttering no reproaches or replies (<reference osisRef="John.19.9">Joh 19:9</reference>) to their insulting speeches; <div eID="gen8987" type="x-p"/>
entries.06fdd59b6bc888dff147c91b7101647246a499fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5912"/><div sID="gen8988" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5912"/>15-17. for he is confident the<div eID="gen8988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord--</hi>literally, "Sovereign" (to whom he was a servant), would answer his prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.4">Psa 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">4:1</reference>), and not permit their triumph in his partial halting, of which he was in danger. <div eID="gen8989" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6c3cfc1e42da67e378bf99edd20a35b3e103c9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5913"/><div sID="gen8990" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5913"/>18. Consciousness of sin makes suffering pungent, and suffering, rightly received, leads to confession. <div eID="gen8990" type="x-p"/>
entries.2fa183f6b7b4726ee50b94971ebf9c0cc3e6106f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5914"/><div sID="gen8991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5914"/>19-20. Still, while humbled before God, he is the victim of deadly enemies, full of malice and treachery.<div eID="gen8991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8992" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enemies are lively--</hi>literally, "of life," who would take my life, that is, deadly. <div eID="gen8992" type="x-p"/>
entries.339c9fdc8d81f8a128f4a6f7809a51f5ae3c7d90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5915"/><div sID="gen8993" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5915"/>21-22. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.22.19">Psa 22:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.3">35:3</reference>). All terms of frequent use. In this Psalm the language is generally susceptible of application to Christ as a sufferer, David, as such, typifying Him. This does not require us to apply the confessions of sin, but only the pains or penalties which He bore for us. <chapter eID="Ps.38"/>

entries.d15cecf0edb8fc609ad12654bf71233da15c5189: <div eID="gen19835" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19836" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19837" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19837" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19836" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19838" type="x-p"/> David prays God to have mercy upon him, and gives a most affecting account of his miserable state, <reference osisRef="Psa.38.1-Psa.38.10">Psa 38:1-10</reference>; complains of his being forsaken by his friends, and cruelly persecuted by his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.38.11-Psa.38.16">Psa 38:11-16</reference>; confesses his sin; and earnestly implores help, <reference osisRef="Psa.38.17-Psa.38.22">Psa 38:17-22</reference>. <div eID="gen19838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19839" type="x-p"/> The title in the Hebrew states this to be A Psalm of David, to bring to remembrance. The Chaldee; "A Psalm of David for a good memorial to Israel." The Vulgate, Septuagint, and Aethiopic: "A Psalm of David, for a commemoration concerning the Sabbath." The Arabic: "A Psalm in which mention is made of the Sabbath; besides, it is a thanksgiving and a prophecy." Never was a title more misplaced or less expressive of the contents. There is no mention of the Sabbath in it; there is no thanksgiving in it, for it is deeply penitential; and I do not see that it contains any prophecy. The Syriac: "A psalm of David, when they said to the Philistine king, Achish, This is David, who killed Goliath; we will not have him to go with us against Saul. Besides, it is a form of confession for us." It does not appear that, out of all the titles, we can gather the true intent of the Psalm. <div eID="gen19839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19840" type="x-p"/> Several conjectures have been made relative to the occasion on which this Psalm was composed; and the most likely is, that it was in reference to some severe affliction which David had after his illicit commerce with Bath-sheba; but of what nature we are left to conjecture from the third, fifth, and seventh verses. Whatever it was, he deeply repents for it, asks pardon, and earnestly entreats support from God. <div eID="gen19840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19841" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19842" type="x-p"/> O Lord, rebuke me not - He was sensible that he was suffering under the displeasure of God; and he prays that the chastisement may be in mercy, and not in judgment.
entries.426f7bb4453b56d7a28b0b51a018746674d01817: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19843" type="x-p"/> Thine arrows stick fast in me - This no doubt, refers to the acute pains which he endured; each appearing to his feeling as if an arrow were shot into his body.
entries.dac8f75911503f3b9a2374f794dc34b15c47ee60: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19844" type="x-p"/> No soundness in my flesh - This seems to refer to some disorder which so affected the muscles as to produce sores and ulcers; and so affected his bones as to leave him no peace nor rest. In short, he was completely and thoroughtly diseased; and all this he attributes to his sin, either as being its natural consequence, or as being inflicted by the Lord as a punishment on its account.
entries.f7827bc37bf6e44da134e0880a3821f886b18d16: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19845" type="x-p"/> Mine iniquities are gone over mine head - He represents himself as one sinking in deep waters, or as one oppressed by a burden to which his strength was unequal.
entries.6e7f60780d56a3915cbdf43d0b460a7361b1c21d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19846" type="x-p"/> My wounds stink and are corrupt - Taking this in connection with the rest of the Psalm, I do not see that we can understand the word in any figurative or metaphorical way. I believe they refer to some disease with which he was at this time afflicted; but whether the leprosy, the small pox, or some other disorder that had attacked the whole system, and showed its virulence on different parts of the outer surface, cannot be absolutely determined. <div eID="gen19846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19847" type="x-p"/> Because of my foolishness - This may either signify sin as the cause of his present affliction, or it may import an affliction which was the consequence of that foolish levity which prefers the momentary gratification of an irregular passion to health of body and peace of mind.
entries.24d6025b6197ba3f7457b950106222e97d04627e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19848" type="x-p"/> I am troubled - In mind. I am bowed down in body. I am altogether afflicted, and full of distress.
entries.36094c9968343a3453bd4353601455e4438bf6f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19849" type="x-p"/> For my loins are filled with a loathsome disease - Or rather, a burning; נקלה nikleh, from קלה kalah, to fry, scorch, etc., hence נקלה nikleh, a burning, or strongly feverish disease. <div eID="gen19849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19850" type="x-p"/> There is no soundness in my flesh - All without and all within bears evidence that the whole of my solids and fluids are corrupt.
entries.cc25819c6aabc4c3f296d519a5e6a5fac181d233: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19851" type="x-p"/> I am feeble and sore broken - I am so exhausted with my disease that I feel as if on the brink of the grave, and unfit to appear before God; therefore "have I roared for the disquietness of my heart." <div eID="gen19851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19852" type="x-p"/> That David describes a natural disease here cannot reasonably be doubted; but what that disease was, who shall attempt to say? However, this is evident, that whatever it was, he most deeply deplored the cause of it; and as he worthily lamented it, so he found mercy at the hand of God. It would be easy to show a disease of which what he here enumerates are the very general symptoms; but I forbear, because in this I might attribute to one what, perhaps, in Judea would be more especially descriptive of another.
entries.3bd89159f4939b0a66149f1e737c0846a22d5f83: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19853" type="x-p"/> Lord, all my desire is before thee - I long for nothing so much as thy favor; and for this my heart is continually going out after thee. Instead of אדני Adonai, Lord, several of Dr. Kennicott's MSS. have יהוה Yehovah.
entries.55aabeb4f5fd054e8b72364e7afbf504e8916ec8: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen19853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19854" type="x-p"/> My heart panteth - סחרחר secharchar, flutters, palpitates, through fear and alarm. <div eID="gen19854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19855" type="x-p"/> My strength faileth - Not being able to take nourishment. <div eID="gen19855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19856" type="x-p"/> The light of mine eyes - is gone - I can scarcely discern any thing through the general decay of my health and vigor, particularly affecting my sight.
entries.15c97969d6b0d8859a628d8072d88c3b92c38af2: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19857" type="x-p"/> My lovers - Those who professed much affection for me; my friends, רעי reai, my companions, who never before left my company, stand aloof. <div eID="gen19857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19858" type="x-p"/> My kinsmen - קרובי kerobai, my neighbors, stand afar off. I am deserted by all, and they stand off because of נגעי nigi, my plague. They considered me as suffering under a Divine judgment; and, thinking me an accursed being, they avoided me lest they should be infected by my disease.
entries.7d2e76b1830315d005f5c989885ea6ccdcda8bd1: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen19858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19859" type="x-p"/> They also that seek after my life - They act towards me as huntsmen after their prey; they lay snares to take away my life. Perhaps this means only that they wished for his death, and would have been glad to have had it in their power to end his days. Others spoke all manner of evil of him, and told falsities against him all the day long.
entries.fa390835df15d05667ab4eabb61064b345520aea: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen19859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19860" type="x-p"/> But I, as a deaf man - I was conscious of my guilt, I could not vindicate myself; and I was obliged in silence to bear their insults.
entries.39ca64fa7b1565346e2df6d485af0ace91f1d661: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen19860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19861" type="x-p"/> No reproofs - תוכחות tochachoth, arguments or vindications; a forensic term. I was as a man accused in open court, and I could make no defense.
entries.6fa21d7c745c2c172f8b8065c75cad74b18a82f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen19861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19862" type="x-p"/> In thee, O Lord, do I hope - I have no helper but thee. <div eID="gen19862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19863" type="x-p"/> Thou wilt hear, O Lord my God - Thou art eternal in thy compassions, and wilt hear the prayer of a penitent soul. In the printed copies of the Hebrew text we have אדני אלהי Adonai Elohai, Lord my God; but, instead of אדני Adonai, one hundred and two of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. read יהוה Yehovah. As this word is never pronounced by the Jews, and they consider it dreadfully sacred, in reading, wherever it occurs, they pronounce אדני Adonai; and we may well suppose that Jewish scribes, in writing out copies of the sacred Scriptures, would as naturally write Adonai for Yehovah, as they would in reading supply the former for the latter.
entries.d8f0dc9a8053623a659f65478276b1ae000f2811: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen19863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19864" type="x-p"/> When my foot slippeth - They watched for my halting; and when my foot slipped, they rejoiced that I had fallen into sin!
entries.90ed44209aaadae596e86f3409dfea510ed6c711: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen19864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19865" type="x-p"/> For I am ready to halt - Literally, I am prepared to halt. So completely infirm is my soul, that it is impossible for me to take one right step in the way of righteousness, unless strengthened by thee.
entries.c58ecd1ede8565977a074414c55db55ec7da9248: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen19865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19866" type="x-p"/> I will declare mine iniquity - I will confess it with the deepest humiliation and self-abasement.
entries.44e8be7c09e7c330ff4c87509eb94ae98f12c972: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen19866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19867" type="x-p"/> But mine enemies are lively - Instead of חיים chaiyim, lively, I would read חינם chinam, without cause; a change made by the half of one letter, נ nun for a י yod. See the parallel places, <reference osisRef="Psa.35.19">Psa 35:19</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Psa.79.5">Psa 79:5</reference> (note). See also the Preliminary Dissertation to Dr. Lowth's Isaiah, p. 40: "But without cause my enemies have strengthened themselves; and they who wrongfully hate me are multiplied." Here the one member of the verse answers to the other.
entries.5dcdf0adb3a7f3fa599356e24b0b5e1805f0801e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen19867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19868" type="x-p"/> Because I follow the thing that good is - The translation is as bad as the sentence is awkward. תחת רדפי טוב tachath rodpi tob, because I follow goodness. There is a remarkable addition to this verse in the Arabic: "They have rejected me, the beloved one, as an abominable dead carcass; they have pierced my body with nails." I suppose the Arabic translator meant to refer this to Christ. <div eID="gen19868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19869" type="x-p"/> None of the other Versions have any thing like this addition; only the Ethiopic adds, "They rejected their brethren as an unclean carcass." St. Ambrose says this reading was found in some Greek and Latin copies in his time; and Theodoret has nearly the same reading with the Arabic: Και απερῥιψαν με τον αγαπητον, ῳς νεκρον εβδελυγμενον· "And they cast me, the beloved, out, as an abominable dead carcass." Whence this reading came I cannot conjecture.
entries.9393ee2a4229989ccd049577bccf08b946862398: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen19869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19870" type="x-p"/> Forsake me not, O Lord - Though all have forsaken me, do not thou. <div eID="gen19870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19871" type="x-p"/> Be not far from me - Though my friends keep aloof, be thou near to help me.
entries.f85c89bfa0afb46d8454fa6785aa0627cbc6d87f: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen19871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19872" type="x-p"/> Make haste to help me - I am dying; save, Lord, or I perish. Whoever carefuIly reads over this Psalm will see what a grievous and bitter thing it is to sin against the Lord, and especially to sin after having known his mercy, and after having escaped from the corruption that is in the world. Reader, be on thy guard; a life of righteousness may be lost by giving way to a moment's temptation, and a fair character sullied for ever! Let him that most assuredly standeth take heed lest he fall. 'Tis but a grain of sweet that one can sow, <div eID="gen19872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19873" type="x-p"/> To reap a harvest of wide-wasting wo.  <chapter eID="Ps.38"/> <div eID="gen19873" type="x-p"/>

entries.3469d16d3e3d3780d148267db61abfa94eb2989a: <div eID="gen9428" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Prayer for the Changing of Merited Wrath into Rescuing Love</title> <div sID="gen9429" type="x-p"/> The Penitential Psalm, 38, is placed immediately after Ps 37 on account of the similarity of its close to the ת strophe of that Psalm. It begins like <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1">Psa 6:1</reference>-10. If we regard David’s adultery as the occasion of it (cf. more especially <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.14">2Sa 12:14</reference>), then Psa 6:1-10; 38; 51; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11">Psa 32:1-11</reference> form a chronological series. David is distressed both in mind and body, forsaken by his friends, and regarded by his foes as one who is cast off for ever. The fire of divine anger burns within him like a fever, and the divine withdrawal as it were rests upon him like darkness. But he fights his way by prayer through this fire and this darkness to the bright confidence of faith. The Psalm, although it is the pouring forth of such elevated and depressed feelings, is nevertheless symmetrically and skilfully laid out. It consists of three main paragraphs, which divide into four (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.2">Psa 38:2</reference>), three (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.10">Psa 38:10</reference>), and four (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.16">Psa 38:16</reference>) tetrastichs. The way in which the names of God are brought in is well conceived. The first word of the first group or paragraph is יהוה, the first word of the second אדני, and in the third יהוה and אדני are used interchangeably twice. The Psalm, in common with <reference osisRef="Ps.70.1-Ps.70.5">Psa 70:1-5</reference>, bears the inscription להזכּיר. The chronicler, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.4">1Ch 16:4</reference>, refers to these <hi type="italic">Hazkir</hi> Psalms together with the <hi type="italic">Hodu</hi> and <hi type="italic">Halleluja</hi> Psalms. In connection with the presentation of meat-offerings, מנחות, a portion of the meat-offering was cast into the altar fire, viz., a handful of the meal mixed with oil and the whole of the incense. This portion was called אזכּרה, ἀνάμνησις, and to offer it הזכּיר (a denominative), because the ascending smoke was intended to bring the owner of the offering into remembrance with God. In connection with the presentation of this memorial portion of the <hi type="italic">mincha</hi>, the two Psalms are appointed to be used as prayers; hence the inscription: <hi type="italic">at the presentation of the Azcara </hi>(the portion taken from the meal-offering). The lxx adds here περὶ (τοῦ) σαββάτου; perhaps equivalent to לשּׁבּת. <div eID="gen9429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9430" type="x-p"/> In this Psalm we find a repetition of a peculiarity of the penitential Psalms, viz., that the praying one has to complain not only of afflictions of body and soul, but also of outward enemies, who come forward as his accusers and take occasion from his sin to prepare the way for his ruin. This arises from the fact that the Old Testament believer, whose perception of sin was not as yet so spiritual and deep as that of the New Testament believer, almost always calls to mind some sinful act that has become openly known. The foes, who would then prepare for his ruin, are the instruments of the Satanic power of evil (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.38.21">Psa 38:21</reference>, ישׂטנוּני), which, as becomes perceptible to the New Testament believer even without the intervention of outward foes, desires the death of the sinning one, whereas God wills that he should live.
entries.db80f1404bafa9396e42e284bb04ef57f1f8abe2: <reference osisRef="Ps.38.1-Ps.38.8">Psa 38:1-8</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_38:2-9) David begins, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1-Ps.6.10">Psa 6:1-10</reference>, with the prayer that his punitive affliction may be changed into disciplinary. Bakius correctly paraphrases. <reference osisRef="Ps.38.2">Psa 38:2</reference> : <hi type="italic">Corripe sane per legem, castiga per crucem, millies promerui, negare non possum, sed castiga, quaeso, me ex amore ut pater, non ex furore et fervore ut judex; ne punias justitiae rigore, sed misericordiae dulcore</hi> (cf. on <reference osisRef="Ps.6.2">Psa 6:2</reference>). The negative is to be repeated in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.38.2">Psa 38:2</reference></hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.1.5">Psa 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.19">Psa 9:19</reference>; Psa 75:6. In the description, which give the ground of the cry for pity, נחת, is not the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.35">Psa 18:35</reference>, but the <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> נחת immediately following (root נח). קצף is anger as a breaking forth, <hi type="italic">fragor</hi> (cf. Hos 10:7, lxx φρύγανον), with <hi type="italic">ĕ</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">ı̆</hi> in the first syllable, vowels which alternate in this word; and חמה, as a glowing or burning. חצּים (in Homer, κῆλα), God’s wrath-arrows, i.e., lightnings of wrath, are His judgments of wrath; and יד, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.4">Psa 32:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.39.11">Psa 39:11</reference>, God’s punishing hand, which makes itself felt in dispensing punishment, hence תּנחת might be attached as a mood of sequence. In <reference osisRef="Ps.38.4">Psa 38:4</reference> wrath is called זעם as a boiling up. Sin is the cause of this experiencing wrath, and the wrath is the cause of the bodily derangement; sin as an exciting cause of the wrath always manifests itself outwardly even on the body as a fatal power. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.38.5">Psa 38:5</reference></hi> sin is compared to waters that threaten to drown one, as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.38.5">Psa 38:5</reference></hi> to a burden that presses one down. ככבּדוּ ממּנּי, they are heavier than I, i.e., than my power of endurance, too heavy for me. In <reference osisRef="Ps.38.6">Psa 38:6</reference> the effects of the operation of the divine hand (as punishing) are wounds, חבּוּרת (properly, suffused variegated marks from a blow or wheals, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Isa 1:6</reference>; from חבר, Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥbr</hi>, to be or make striped, variegated), which הבאישׁוּ, send forth an offensive smell, and נמקּוּ, suppurate. Sin, which causes this, is called אוּלת, because, as it is at last manifest, it is always the destruction of itself. With emphasis does מפּני אוּלתּי form the second half of the verse. To take נעויתי out of <reference osisRef="Ps.38.7">Psa 38:7</reference> and put it to this, as Meier and Thenius propose, is to destroy this its proper position. On the three מפּני, vid., Ewald, §217, <hi type="italic">l</hi>. Thus sick in soul and body, he is obliged to bow and bend himself in the extreme. נעוה is used of a convulsive drawing together of the body, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.3">Isa 21:3</reference>; שׁחח, of a bowed mien, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.14">Psa 35:14</reference>; הלּך, of a heavy, lagging gait. With כּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.38.8">Psa 38:8</reference> the grounding of the petition begins for the third time. His כּסלים, i.e., internal muscles of the loins, which are usually the fattest parts, are full of נקלה, that which is burnt, i.e., parched. It is therefore as though the burning, starting from the central point of the bodily power, would spread itself over the whole body: the wrath of God works commotion in this latter as well as in the soul. Whilst all the energies of life thus yield, there comes over him a partial, almost total lifelessness. פּוּג is the proper word for the coldness and rigidity of a corpse; the <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> means to be brought into this condition, just as נדכּא means to be crushed, or to be brought into a condition of crushing, i.e., of violent dissolution. The מן of מנּהמת is intended to imply that the loud wail is only the utterance of the pain that is raging in his heart, the outward expression of his ceaseless, deep inward groaning.
entries.acbbfd9a3fd3baa86dabac45df5462fe91e4768b: <reference osisRef="Ps.38.9-Ps.38.14">Psa 38:9-14</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_38:10-15) Having thus bewailed his suffering before God, he goes on in a somewhat calmer tone: it is the calm of weariness, but also of the rescue which shows itself from afar. He has complained, but not as if it were necessary for him first of all to make God acquainted with his suffering; the Omniscient One is directly cognisant of (has directly before Him, נגד, like לנגד in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.25">Psa 18:25</reference>) every wish that his suffering extorts from him, and even his softer sighing does not escape His knowledge. The sufferer does not say this so much with the view of comforting himself with this thought, as of exciting God’s compassion. Hence he even goes on to draw the piteous picture of his condition: his heart is in a state of violent rotary motion, or only of violent, quickly repeated contraction and expansion (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 252; tr. p. 297), that is to say, a state of violent palpitation (סחרחר, <hi type="italic">Pealal</hi> according to Ges. §55, 3). Strength of which the heart is the centre (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.13">Psa 40:13</reference>) has left him, and the light of his eyes, even of these (by attraction for גּם־הוּא, since the light of the eyes is not contrasted with anything else), is not with him, but has become lost to him by weeping, watching, and fever. Those who love him and are friendly towards him have placed themselves far from his stroke (nega`, the touch of God’s hand of wrath), merely looking on (Oba 1:11), therefore, in a position hostile (<reference osisRef="2Sam.18.13">2Sa 18:13</reference>) rather than friendly. מנּגד, far away, but within the range of vision, within sight, <reference osisRef="Gen.21.16">Gen 21:16</reference>; Deu 32:52. The words וּקרובי מרחק עמדוּ, which introduce a pentastich into a Psalm that is tetrastichic throughout, have the appearance of being a gloss or various reading: מנּגד = מרחק, 2Ki 2:7. His enemies, however, endeavour to take advantage of his fall and helplessness, in order to give him his final death-blow. וינקּשׁוּ (with the ק dageshed)<note placement="foot">The various reading וינקּשׁוּ in Norzi rests upon a misapprehended passage of Abulwalîd (<hi type="italic">Rikma</hi>, p. 166).</note> describes what they have planned in consequence of the position he is in. The substance of their words is הוּות, utter destruction (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.5.10">Psa 5:10</reference>); to this end it is מרמות, deceit upon deceit, malice upon malice, that they unceasingly hatch with heart and mouth. In the consciousness of his sin he is obliged to be silent, and, renouncing all self-help, to abandon his cause to God. Consciousness of guilt and resignation close his lips, so that he is not able, nor does he wish, to refute the false charges of his enemies; he has no תּוכחות, counter-evidence wherewith to vindicate himself. It is not to be rendered: “just as one dumb opens not his mouth;” כ is only a preposition, not a conjunction, and it is just here, in <reference osisRef="Ps.38.14">Psa 38:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.15">Psa 38:15</reference>, that the manifest proofs in support of this are found.<note placement="foot">The passages brought forward by Hupfeld in support of the use of כ as a conjunction, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.90.5">Psa 90:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.125.1">Psa 125:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">Isa 53:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.11">Isa 61:11</reference>, are invalid; the passage that seems most to favour it is Oba 1:16, but in this instance the expression is elliptical, כּלא being equivalent to כאשׁר לא, like ללא, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.1">Isa 65:1</reference>, = לאשׁר לא. It is only כּמו (Arab. <hi type="italic">kmâ</hi>) that can be used as a conjunction; but כ (Arab. <hi type="italic">k</hi>) is always a preposition in ancient Hebrew just as in Syriac and Arabic (vid., Fleischer in the <hi type="italic">Hallische Allgem. Lit. Zeitschr.</hi> 1843, Bd. iv. S. 117ff.). It is not until the mediaeval synagogal poetry (vid., Zunz, <hi type="italic">Synagogal-poesie des Mittelalters</hi>, S. 121, 381f.) that it is admissible to use it as a conjunction (e.g., כּמצא, when he had found), just as it also occurs in Himjaritic, according to Osiander’s deciphering of the inscriptions. The verbal clause appended to the word to which this כ, <hi type="italic">instar</hi>, is prefixed is for the most part an attributive clause as above, but sometimes even a circumstantial clause (Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥâl</hi>), as in <reference osisRef="Ps.38.14">Psa 38:14</reference>; cf. <hi type="italic">Sur</hi>. lxii. 5: “as the likeness of an ass carrying books.”</note>
entries.6f419dd53248dc53d864454507fe5f8a0fda2bad: <reference osisRef="Ps.38.15-Ps.38.22">Psa 38:15-22</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_38:16-23) Become utterly useless in himself, he renounces all self-help, for (כּי) he hopes in Jahve, who alone can help him. He waits for His answer, for (כי) he says, etc. - he waits for an answer, for the hearing of this his petition which is directed towards the glory of God, that God would not suffer his foes to triumph over him, nor strengthen them in their mercilessness and injustice. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.38.18">Psa 38:18</reference></hi> appears also to stand under the government of the פּן;<note placement="foot">The following are the constructions of פן when a clause of ore than one member follows it: (1) <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. and <hi type="italic">perf</hi>., the latter with the tone of the <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>., e.g., Exo 34:15., or without it, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Psa 28:1</reference> (which see); (2) <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. and <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">Psa 2:12</reference>, Jer 51:46. This construction is indispensable where it is intended to give special prominence to the subject notion or a secondary notion of the clause, e.g., Deu 20:6. In one instance פן is even followed (3) by the <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. and <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>., viz., 2Ki 2:10.</note> but, since in this case one would look for a <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> <hi type="italic">relat</hi>. and a different order of the words, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.38.18">Psa 38:18</reference></hi> is to be regarded as a subject clause: “who, when my foot totters, i.e., when my affliction changes to entire downfall, would magnify themselves against me.” In <reference osisRef="Ps.38.18">Psa 38:18</reference>,   כּי connects what follows with בּמוט רגלי by way of confirmation: he is נכון לצלע, ready for falling (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.15">Psa 35:15</reference>), he will, if God does not graciously interpose, assuredly fall headlong. The fourth כּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.38.19">Psa 38:19</reference> is attached confirmatorily to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.38.18">Psa 38:18</reference></hi>: his intense pain or sorrow is ever present to him, for he is obliged to confess his guilt, and this feeling of guilt is just the very sting of his pain. And whilst he in the consciousness of well-deserved punishment is sick unto death, his foes are numerous and withal vigorous and full of life. Instead of חיּים, probably חנּם, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.19">Psa 35:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.5">Psa 69:5</reference>, is to be read (Houbigant, Hitzig, Köster, Hupfeld, Ewald, and Olshausen). But even the lxx read חיים; and the reading which is so old, although it does not very well suit עצמוּ (instead of which one would look for ועצוּמים), is still not without meaning: he looks upon himself, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.38.9">Psa 38:9</reference>, more as one dead than living; his foes, however, are חיּים, living, i.e., vigorous. The verb frequently ash this pregnant meaning, and the adjective can also have it. Just as the accentuation of the form סבּוּ varies elsewhere out of pause, ורבּוּ here has the tone on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>, although it is not <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>.<note placement="foot">As <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>. the following have the accent on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>: - וחתּוּ, <reference osisRef="Isa.20.5">Isa 20:5</reference>, Oba 1:9, and ורבּוּ, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.16">Isa 66:16</reference>; perhaps also וחדּוּ, וקלּוּ, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.8">Hab 1:8</reference>, and ורבּוּ (<hi type="italic">perf. hypoth</hi>.), Job 32:15. But there is no special reason for the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>-accentuation of רכּוּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.22">Psa 55:22</reference>; רבּוּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.5">Psa 69:5</reference>; דּלּוּ, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.14">Isa 38:14</reference>; קלּוּ, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.13">Jer 4:13</reference>; שׁחוּ, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.19">Pro 14:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Hab 3:6</reference>; חתּוּ, <reference osisRef="Job.32.15">Job 32:15</reference>; זכּוּ, צחוּ, Lam 4:7.</note><hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.38.21">Psa 38:21</reference></hi> is an apposition of the subject, which remains the same as in Psa 38:20. Instead of רדופי (Ges. §61, rem. 2) the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> is רדפי, <hi type="italic">rādephî</hi>  (without any <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> following), or רדפי, <hi type="italic">rādophî</hi>; cf. on this pronunciation, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.2">Psa 86:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference>, and with the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> רדופי, the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> צרופה, <reference osisRef="Ps.26.2">Psa 26:2</reference>, also מיורדי, Psa 30:4. By the “following of that which is good” David means more particularly that which is brought into exercise in relation to his present foes.<note placement="foot">In the Greek and Latin texts, likewise in all the Aethiopic and several Arabic texts, and in the Syriac <hi type="italic">Psalterium Medilanense</hi>, the following addition is found after <reference osisRef="Ps.38.21">Psa 38:21</reference> : <hi type="italic">Ce aperripsan me ton agapeton osi necron ebdelygmenon, Et projecerunt me dilectum tanquam mortuum abominatum</hi> (so the <hi type="italic">Psalt. Veronense</hi>). Theodoret refers it to Absalom’s relation to David. The words ὡσεὶ νεκρὸν ἐβδελυγμένον are taken from Isa 14:19.</note> <div eID="gen9430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9431" type="x-p"/> He closes in <reference osisRef="Ps.38.22">Psa 38:22</reference> with sighs for help. No lighting up of the darkness of wrath takes place. The <hi type="italic">fides supplex</hi> is not changed into <hi type="italic">fides triumphans</hi>. But the closing words, “O Lord, my salvation” (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.16">Psa 51:16</reference>), show where the repentance of Cain and that of David differ. True repentance has faith within itself, it despairs of itself, but not of God.  <chapter eID="Ps.38"/> <div eID="gen9431" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 38
David, suffering under some severe and dangerous malady, as may be conjectured, acknowledges that he is chastened by the Lord, and entreats him to turn away his anger from him. In order the more effectually to induce God to have mercy upon him, he bewails before him the severity of his afflictions in a variety of particulars. These we shall consider separately, and in order.
A Psalm of David to bring to remembrance.
This title occurs only here and in the 70th psalm. This psalm is the third of what are called the Penitential Psalms. The two before this are the 6th and the 32d; and the four which follow it are the 51st, the 102d, the 130th, and the 143d. It is a curious fact, that when Galileo was sentenced to be confined in the dungeons of the Inquisition for an indefinite period, for having maintained the Copernican system, he was enjoined to repeat as a penance these seven Penitential Psalms every week for three years; by which it was doubtless intended to extort a sort of confession from him of his guilt, and an acknowledgement of the justice of his sentence.
The title of this psalm refers to its subject. Some suppose that it is the beginning of a common song, because in other psalms the beginning of the song, to the tune of which they were set, is commonly prefixed: but such an interpretation is unnatural, and without foundation. Instead of this, I rather think that the title indicates that David composed this psalm as a memorial for himself, as well as others, lest he should too soon forget the chastisement by which God had afflicted him. He knew how easily and speedily the chastisements with which God visits us, and which ought to serve as a means of instruction to us all our life, pass away from the mind. He was also mindful of his own high calling; for, as he was appointed master and teacher over the whole Church, it was necessary that whatever he had himself learned in particular by divine teaching should be made known, and appropriated to the use of all, that all might profit thereby. Thus we are admonished that it is a very profitable exercise often to recall to remembrance the chastisements with which God has afflicted us for our sins.
Psalm 38:1-5
1. O Jehovah! rebuke me not in thy wrath, and chasten me not in thy anger. 2. For thy arrows go down in me
That is, they enter deep into the flesh. The Septuagint reads, “Ενεπάγησάν μοι” the Vulgate, “Infixae sunt mihi;” — “Are fastened in me;” which is a natural consequence of entering deep, and rather expresses the meaning, than conveys the precise idea of the original word. The Syriac and Arabic versions give the same rendering with the Vulgate.
and thy hand has come down upon me. 3. There is no soundness in my flesh because of thy anger; nor any peace in my bones because of my sin. 4. For my iniquities have passed over my head, and as a weighty burden they have become too heavy for me. 5. My wounds have become putrid, they are corrupt, because of my foolishness.
 
1 O Jehovah! rebuke me not in thy wrath As I have already expounded this verse in the beginning of the sixth psalm, where it occurs, and that I may not prove tedious to the reader, I shall notice it more briefly here. David does not expressly ask that his afflictions should be removed, but only that God would moderate the severity of his chastisements. Hence we may infer, that David did not give loose reins to the desires of the flesh, but offered up his earnest prayer in a duly chastened spirit of devotion. All men would naturally desire that permission should be granted them to sin with impunity. But David lays a restraint upon his desires, and does not wish the favor and indulgence of God to be extended beyond measure, but is content with a mitigation of his affliction; as if he had said, Lord, I am not unwilling to be chastised by thee, but I entreat thee, meanwhile, not to afflict me beyond what I am able to bear, but to temper the fierceness of thy indignation according to the measure of my infirmity, lest the severity of the affliction should entirely overwhelm me. This prayer, as I have said, was framed according to the rule of godliness; for it contains nothing but what God promises to all his children. It should also be noticed, that David does not secretly indulge a fretful and repining spirit, but spreads his complaint before God; and this he does, not in the way of sinful complaining, but of humble prayer and unfeigned confession, accompanied with the hope of obtaining forgiveness. He has used anger and wrath as denoting extreme rigour, and has contrasted them with fatherly chastisement.

                     <ns0:p>This is reckoned one of <ns0:hi>David'</ns0:hi>s penitential <ns0:hi>Psalms.</ns0:hi> It was Composed upon occasion of some sore Disease, or grievous Calamity; which he rightly judged to be inflicted upon him for his sins.</ns0:p>

                     <ns0:hi>A Psalm</ns0:hi> of David to bring <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 70. Tit.</ns0:note> to remembrance <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either, 1. To himself, that by reviewing this Psalm afterwards, he might call to Mind his former Danger and Misery, and God's wonderful mercy in delivering him from them; which we are very apt to forget. Poole.heading:
PSAL. XXXVIII. 
                     A Psalm of David to bring Psal. 70. Tit. to remembrance Either, 1. To God, that by this humble and mournful Prayer, he might prevail with God, to remember and Pity him; for now he seemed, quite to have forgotten him. Or, 2. To himself, that by reviewing this Psalm afterwards, he might call to Mind his former Danger and Misery, and God's wonderful mercy in delivering him from them; which we are very apt to forget. And that others also might remember and consider what God had done to him, first in Chastening, and then in restoring him, and might make use of his Example for their benefit..
